title: Coin Change Problem
description: Learn how greedy coin selection minimizes resource usage and understand when greedy optimization succeeds or fails.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Coin Change Problem is one of the most common applications of Greedy Algorithms.

The objective is to find the minimum number of coins needed to make a target amount.

Instead of trying every possible combination, the greedy strategy repeatedly selects the largest coin denomination available.

This problem introduces learners to greedy optimization, local decision making, resource minimization, and algorithmic efficiency.

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Cashier systems, vending machines, banking software, and digital payment systems constantly calculate efficient ways to return change.

Giving many small coins may technically work, but it becomes inefficient and inconvenient. The Coin Change Problem models how systems minimize resource usage through optimization.
bullets: Minimizes the number of coins used.

sections.title: Core Idea of the Greedy Strategy
sections.content:
The greedy approach follows one simple rule: always choose the largest possible coin at the current step.

After selecting a coin, the algorithm subtracts its value from the remaining amount and repeats the process again.

This continues until the remaining amount becomes zero.

sections.title: Understanding Greedy Coin Selection
sections.content:
Suppose we need to make 18 pesos using coins 10, 5, and 1.

The algorithm first selects 10 because it is the largest usable coin. The remaining amount becomes 8.

Next, the algorithm selects 5, reducing the remaining amount to 3.

Finally, the algorithm uses three 1-peso coins.

The final solution becomes 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1.

sections.title: Why the Greedy Strategy Works Here
sections.content:
The greedy strategy succeeds because larger denominations reduce the remaining amount quickly.

Choosing large coins first usually minimizes unnecessary smaller denominations and reduces the total coin count.

Many real-world currency systems are designed so greedy coin selection works correctly.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Visualization
sections.content:
Suppose we need to make 36 using coins 25, 10, 5, and 1.

The algorithm selects 25 first, leaving 11 remaining.

Next, the algorithm selects 10, leaving 1 remaining.

Finally, the algorithm selects 1.

The final solution becomes 25 + 10 + 1, using only 3 coins.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: Greedy Coin Change implementations repeatedly select the largest possible denomination until the target amount becomes zero.

codeSnippets.title: Greedy Coin Change implementation
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [25, 10, 5, 1]
amount = 36
selected = []

for coin in coins:
    while amount >= coin:
        selected.append(coin)
        amount -= coin

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Count total coins used
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [10, 5, 1]
amount = 18
count = 0

for coin in coins:
    while amount >= coin:
        amount -= coin
        count += 1

print(count)

codeSnippets.title: Track remaining amount
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [25, 10, 5, 1]
amount = 41

for coin in coins:
    while amount >= coin:
        print('Use:', coin)
        amount -= coin
        print('Remaining:', amount)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Traversing the coin denominations requires O(n) time, where n represents the number of coin types.

In the worst case, the algorithm may repeatedly subtract small denominations such as 1 until the amount becomes zero.

This creates worst-case behavior proportional to the target amount.

Space complexity is usually O(1) because only a small number of variables are required.

chart.title: Greedy Coin Change complexity
chart.description: Greedy Coin Change often scales efficiently because the algorithm immediately commits to large denominations instead of exploring every combination.

sections.title: When Greedy Coin Change Fails
sections.content:
Greedy solutions do not always guarantee optimal answers.

Suppose the available coins are 1, 3, and 4, and the target amount is 6.

The greedy strategy selects 4 first, leaving 2 remaining. The algorithm then uses two 1-peso coins, producing 3 coins total.

However, the optimal solution is 3 + 3, which uses only 2 coins.

This demonstrates that local optimal choices may sometimes produce globally suboptimal solutions.

sections.title: Why Some Currency Systems Work Well
sections.content:
Many real-world currency systems are intentionally designed so greedy coin selection consistently produces optimal solutions.

These are called canonical coin systems.

Examples include many international currencies and common coin denominations used in modern financial systems.

sections.title: Greedy vs Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
Greedy Coin Change prioritizes efficiency by making immediate locally optimal decisions.

Dynamic Programming explores many subproblems and revisits earlier states to guarantee optimal solutions.

Greedy methods are usually faster and use less memory, while Dynamic Programming provides stronger correctness guarantees.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Coin Change logic appears in cashier systems, ATM machines, vending machines, banking software, financial optimization systems, and payment processing platforms.

Many resource minimization problems use similar greedy reasoning strategies.

subsections.title: Mistake: Assuming greedy always produces optimal solutions
subsections.content: Some coin systems break greedy correctness and require Dynamic Programming instead.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring coin ordering
subsections.content: The greedy strategy depends on descending denomination order.

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing greedy optimization with exhaustive search
subsections.content: Greedy algorithms do not test every possibility. They commit immediately to local decisions.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The Coin Change Problem minimizes the number of coins used.
Greedy Coin Change repeatedly selects the largest denomination possible.
Local optimal choices may or may not produce global optimality.
Some currency systems are designed for greedy correctness.
Greedy algorithms are fast and memory efficient.
Dynamic Programming is used when greedy solutions fail.
